name: Lanzhou
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Lanzhou: petrochemical and metals counterparties, northwest logistics and partner diligence in Gansu.
hero_lede: Lanzhou is the capital of Gansu Province and a long-established base for petrochemicals, non-ferrous metals and equipment manufacturing, as well as a rail and logistics crossroads for northwest China. TDSC scopes Lanzhou matters around counterparty and partner diligence, project and supplier integrity, and research supporting disputes.
intro: Lanzhou is the capital of Gansu Province, a city of about 4.45 million residents at the end of 2025 spread across five districts and three counties covering 13,100 square kilometres along the Yellow River. Its industrial base was built around chemical and petrochemical plants, and today the city lists petrochemicals, machinery and equipment manufacturing, non-ferrous metallurgy, energy and power, biomedicine and building materials as its main sectors. Lanzhou is one of China's designated logistics hubs on the New Eurasian Land Bridge, with Lanzhouxi Railway Station as a major western passenger hub. Lanzhou New Area, approved by the State Council in 2012 as the first state-level new area in northwest China, hosts the airport and new industrial and logistics zones.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Lanzhou mainly when buying from, selling to or investing alongside companies in Gansu's heavy industry and energy sectors. Many significant counterparties are state-owned or linked to provincial and municipal governments, and understanding ownership, control and political connections is central. Metals, chemicals and energy trading carries payment, quality and diversion risk. Infrastructure, new energy and industrial park projects in Lanzhou New Area involve local partners, subsidies and land arrangements that need checking. Freight routes toward Central Asia raise customs and sanctions questions. Investigative work must also respect China's strict rules on data, state secrets and cross-border transfer of information.

matters.title: State-linked counterparty diligence
matters.text: Researching Lanzhou petrochemical, metals and equipment companies before supply, offtake or investment agreements, mapping shareholders of record, state-owned and government links, affiliated companies, administrative penalties, litigation, enforcement listings and adverse media, so clients understand who controls the counterparty and what approvals may matter.

matters.title: Metals and chemicals trade risk
matters.text: Checking buyers, sellers and intermediaries in non-ferrous metals, chemicals and energy trades involving Gansu for registration, capacity to perform, related parties, payment and quality disputes, and links to sanctioned persons or end uses, before letters of credit are opened or cargo is released.

matters.title: Project and joint venture partners
matters.text: Reviewing local partners, contractors and consultants in new energy, industrial park and infrastructure projects in Lanzhou New Area and wider Gansu for ownership, track record, government relationships, subsidy and land history and integrity concerns, before commitments are made or during a project review.

matters.title: Northwest overland logistics
matters.text: Supporting compliance teams that route goods through Lanzhou toward Central Asia and Europe, with research on freight forwarders, consolidators and consignees, their ownership and trading history, and indicators of transshipment or export-control evasion, to be assessed with the client's trade counsel.

matters.title: Asset research for enforcement
matters.text: Assisting counsel holding judgments or awards against Gansu companies with research on corporate assets, subsidiaries, equity holdings, enforcement history and changes in shareholders or legal representatives drawn from public registration and court enforcement information, to inform recognition and enforcement strategy.

local_context.title: Courts sitting in Lanzhou
local_context.text: As provincial capital, Lanzhou is the seat of the Gansu High People's Court and of the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court, which handles significant first-instance commercial cases and appeals from district courts in the city. In January 2019 an intellectual property court was inaugurated as a division of the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court, then the eighteenth such tribunal in China. No international commercial tribunal has been identified in Gansu.

local_context.title: Arbitration in Lanzhou
local_context.text: Lanzhou has a local arbitration commission established under China's Arbitration Law, which handles domestic commercial disputes. Foreign-related contracts with Gansu companies more often name CIETAC or an institution in Beijing, Shanghai or abroad. Lanzhou University's law school has hosted China Arbitration Week events with CIETAC and other institutions, reflecting regional interest in commercial arbitration. Enforcement of awards against local parties generally runs through the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court.

local_context.title: Lanzhou New Area
local_context.text: Lanzhou New Area was approved by the State Council on 20 August 2012 as China's fifth state-level new area and the first in the northwest. It covers about 1,744 square kilometres some 70 kilometres north of the city centre and includes Zhongchuan airport, industrial zones and an airport-linked logistics zone. It has been designated a green finance reform pilot zone, relevant to the funding structure of local projects.

local_context.title: Registration and provincial authorities
local_context.text: Companies in Lanzhou are registered with the municipal and district market regulation authorities, and their basic registration, shareholder of record, penalty and abnormal operation information appears in the national enterprise credit information system. Provincial bodies in Lanzhou, including Gansu's market regulation, development and reform and state-owned assets supervision authorities, publish approvals and announcements that help establish state ownership and project status.

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Lanzhou matters from Nashville and has no office or staff in China. Engagements are scoped first against Chinese law on personal information, data security and state secrets, and against US export-control and sanctions screening where trade routes or end users require it. Research then draws on lawful public sources: national enterprise credit and court information, provincial and municipal government announcements, listed-company disclosures, Chinese-language media and industry publications. TDSC does not obtain non-public government records or use pretexts. Where local enquiries are required, TDSC coordinates appropriately qualified professionals and agrees method and data handling with the client's PRC counsel, including how findings may lawfully leave China.

faqs.q: Can TDSC tell whether a Lanzhou counterparty is state-owned?
faqs.a: Often. Shareholders of record in public registration data, provincial and municipal state-owned assets announcements, group websites and disclosures of listed parents usually reveal state ownership. Indirect or nominee holdings and informal government influence are harder to establish, so reports set out the chain that has been documented and where the evidence stops.

faqs.q: Where would a commercial dispute with a Lanzhou company be heard?
faqs.a: Depending on the contract and amount, before a district court in Lanzhou, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court or the Gansu High People's Court, or in arbitration. Intellectual property cases may go to the Lanzhou intellectual property court. Foreign-related contracts often choose CIETAC or an offshore seat. TDSC supports counsel with factual research, not legal advice.

faqs.q: Can you help screen freight routed through Lanzhou toward Central Asia?
faqs.a: Yes. TDSC researches forwarders, consignees and end users in the chain for ownership, trading history, links to sanctioned or restricted parties and indicators of diversion, and reports risks to the client's trade compliance team and counsel. TDSC does not access customs or carrier systems that are not public.

faqs.q: Are there limits on investigative work in Gansu?
faqs.a: Yes. Chinese law restricts collection of personal information, treats some economic data as sensitive and controls transfer of certain information abroad. Commercial investigation is not a recognised licensed profession, and surveillance or pretexting is not used. Engagements are scoped with PRC counsel and limited to lawful public sources and properly authorised enquiries.

faqs.q: Can assets of a Gansu company be traced for enforcement?
faqs.a: Public information often shows subsidiaries, equity holdings, registered capital changes, prior enforcement cases and listings of dishonest judgment debtors. Bank balances and non-public property data are not accessible to TDSC. Findings help counsel judge where recognition and enforcement through the Lanzhou courts may be productive.
